title: Answering the brief without exceeding the evidence
provenance: Original fictional practice commissioned for this curriculum; not authentic IELTS, not standardised or score-calibrated. No third-party text or diagrams used.
license: CC BY 4.0 for original text and SVG; no audio rights or audio files supplied.
word_count_method: Regex word tokens including hyphenated forms; excludes speaker labels, titles, question text and Q locators.

planning_only.note: Text-based estimate only. Future rendition must fit 32 minutes including part pauses; if not, revise the timetable before release.

tasks.task: Future continuous first listen, including planned part pauses
Submit first answers and confidence, without a second play
Four Q-located intensive segments, 15 minutes each

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Communication centre, how can I help?

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: Our neighbourhood group wants advice on preparing a short information sheet. We saw workshops on public speaking and leaflet design, and the second one seems more relevant.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Is leaflet design the subject you want on the booking?

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: Yes, leaflet design. We're not trying to produce a campaign video or a presentation. We need a page that helps visitors understand a local activity and decide what to do next.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Then that workshop should address the kind of decisions you're making. It covers the relationship between a brief, the reader's needs and the information a finished page actually supplies.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: The available date is the twenty-fourth of June.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: I wrote down the seventeenth after a meeting with our group. Was that wrong?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: It was the original proposed date, but we moved the workshop after confirming the room. The twenty-fourth is now fixed.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: That gives us a little more preparation time. I'll update the shared calendar and remove the old notice from the folder.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Please use the confirmation we send today for any travel arrangements.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: I will. Otherwise people may remember that the date changed without remembering which version was the final one, especially if both notices remain visible in the same place.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: What time should we expect the teaching to begin?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Two ten in the afternoon. You can check in shortly before that, but two ten is the session start.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: I had assumed two thirty because another workshop uses that time.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: This one is earlier. We need the opening minutes to discuss the example brief before participants begin revising it.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: Then I'll write two ten clearly and avoid copying the other event's timetable.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Thank you. Similar workshop names can lead people to transfer details from one booking to another, so the confirmation identifies both the subject and the time rather than relying on a general programme heading.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: How many people will attend?

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: Six volunteers helped with the current leaflet, but only four can come to the workshop. Please reserve four places.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Four are available. Will those participants be able to bring the other volunteers' questions?

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: Yes, we'll collect questions beforehand, but we won't treat the two absent volunteers as extra attendees.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: That works. If the attendance changes, tell us rather than making an informal substitution without updating the booking.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: I'll keep one current list. It's useful for our group as well, because we need to know who will report back and who still needs the notes from the session afterwards.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: What is the total fee?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: For those four places, the community-group total is forty-eight pounds.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: Forty-eight for the whole booking?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Yes. It isn't forty-eight for each person. The fee includes the example materials used during the workshop.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: I'll tell our treasurer the total and the number of places together.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Please check both on the confirmation before paying. If the document shows something different, ask us to correct it.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: We will. A clear booking record matters when the person arranging the event and the person making the payment weren't both present for the same conversation.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: Should we bring printed copies of our current leaflet?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: You may, but the essential document is the brief that your group was given. We need to see what the page was supposed to achieve before discussing its appearance.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: I'll bring the brief, including the audience and required information.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Good. If the brief contains an unresolved question, leave that visible rather than quietly fill it with an assumption.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: That could be useful in itself. We've spent time disagreeing about colours when the more important problem may be that we haven't agreed what visitors need to learn from the page or which details are compulsory.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: Will the leader rewrite the whole leaflet for us?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: The workshop helps participants make and explain their own revisions. The leader can clarify the method and discuss examples, but it isn't a commissioned design service.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: So we should expect to leave with a better approach and some tested changes, rather than a guaranteed finished publication.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Exactly. The amount completed depends partly on the material you bring and the questions that arise.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: That sounds reasonable. We'd rather understand why a change is useful than accept a polished page we can't adapt when the activity details change next month.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: Can we use photographs from an earlier event in the exercise?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Bring only material your group is entitled to use for the intended workshop purpose, and keep any conditions visible. The session doesn't give new permission to publish somebody else's work.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: We can use our own prepared sample and discuss a separate permission question if necessary.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Good. The leader can help you identify where a decision is needed, but don't assume that including an image in a draft settles the rights for every later audience.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: We'll distinguish material for the learning exercise from material already cleared for our public leaflet, so the two don't become confused.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: If we have an accessibility requirement, should that be recorded with the booking?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Yes. Describe the practical requirement in your reply so we can discuss the format of the materials and available arrangements.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: One volunteer uses a larger text setting and may prefer a digital copy.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Tell us that, and we will explain what can be supplied. We shouldn't make a general promise before checking the particular format.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: I'll send the details rather than assume a larger printed page is the only option.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Thank you. The conversation should help the participant decide whether the arrangement works, while giving the team enough time to prepare what has been agreed.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: How do we know which version of the joining instructions to use?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: The numbered confirmation is the current version. If a practical detail changes, we'll send a direct revision with the same booking reference. Please replace the earlier instruction rather than combine parts of two messages.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: I'll keep the latest version in our shared folder and mark the previous one as superseded.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: That's helpful. If anything in the update is unclear, ask before the day.

turns.speaker: Applicant
turns.text: We will. A short clarification now is easier than four people arriving at different entrances because each retained a different fragment of the instructions.

turns.speaker: Design host
turns.text: Welcome to the design centre. The diagram places north at the top, with the entrance on the southern edge and the open court in the centre. The eight lettered spaces are destinations around that fixed landmark. Reception is directly south of the court, on the entrance axis. It isn't the room in the south-east corner. Please check in there before joining your workshop. Staff can confirm the group and identify any practical update. A familiar room number from a previous visit may no longer apply, so use today's instructions rather than assuming every activity with a similar title takes place in the same part of the centre.

turns.speaker: Design host
turns.text: The briefing room is directly north of the court. On the diagram it occupies the northern central position between the two northern corners. Your workshop begins there with the example task and the criteria for the exercise. The room is not in the north-west corner, where an earlier programme placed this introduction. We moved the briefing to the northern central room so the group can use a larger shared display. Please wait for the leader before moving the chairs, since the arrangement supports the opening comparison. If you need another position to see the material comfortably, ask so that the group can adjust it deliberately.

turns.speaker: Design host
turns.text: The sample display is directly west of the court, level with its centre. It is not in the south-west area. The display includes several versions of the same information page, with notes about the different briefs they were designed to answer. A page that works well for one audience may be unsuitable for another, so please read the brief beside each example before deciding which version is best. The display is intended to support comparison, not to provide a single style that everyone must copy. You can note a useful feature while also explaining the condition that makes it useful, such as the reader's prior knowledge or the action the page asks them to take.

turns.speaker: Design host
turns.text: The reader-testing room is in the north-east corner, directly east of the briefing room. Both are on the same northern row, so the testing room is not north-east of the briefing room itself. It is north of the space directly east of the court. In that room, participants can try an agreed task with a volunteer reader and observe how the page is interpreted. The exercise is short and has a defined purpose. Please don't add personal questions simply because a reader is willing to talk. The leader will explain what is recorded and how the comments connect to the design question being investigated.

turns.speaker: Design host
turns.text: The resource collection point is in the south-east corner. It lies south of the space directly east of the court and east of reception. You can collect the current worksheet and any approved sample materials there after the briefing. Please check the version label rather than taking the first loose sheet you find. A page from an earlier workshop may ask for a different output or use different criteria. If the supply of a material runs out, tell the helper instead of removing something from another group's working table. The collection point completes the five locations needed for today's activity: reception, briefing, sample display, reader testing and resources.

turns.speaker: Design host
turns.text: A design brief can contain both requirements and suggestions. Requirements describe what the response must achieve or include; suggestions may offer one possible way of doing it. Treating every suggestion as compulsory can overload a short page. Treating a requirement as optional can leave an attractive page unable to do its job. During the workshop, identify the wording that supports your interpretation and ask about a genuine ambiguity. The exercise isn't a test of how confidently you can defend a first guess. It is an opportunity to make the relationship between the brief and your response visible, so a later reviewer can understand why a particular choice was made.

turns.speaker: Design host
turns.text: When reviewing a page, begin with its intended reader and action. A visitor who needs to find a meeting point may not benefit from a long history of the organisation at the top of the page. That history could be interesting, but the task may require it to be shortened or moved. This doesn't mean background information is always unnecessary. It means relevance depends on the purpose and the reader's situation. The workshop asks you to justify the allocation of space, not merely reduce the number of words. A short page can still waste attention if its most prominent information does not help the reader complete the intended action.

turns.speaker: Design host
turns.text: If a figure in your draft lacks a reliable source, mark the gap instead of inventing a plausible number. A realistic-looking figure can be especially misleading because readers may assume someone has checked it. You can explain what information is missing and how it affects the claim. In some cases the responsible revision is to remove or qualify a statement until evidence is available. The leader won't reward a complete-looking page at the expense of accuracy. This principle also applies to examples: a hypothetical illustration should remain identified as hypothetical, rather than becoming an apparent report of an event simply because it makes the layout easier to finish.

turns.speaker: Design host
turns.text: Reader testing should distinguish what a person does from your explanation of why they do it. If a reader opens the wrong section, record the action before deciding that the heading caused the problem. They may have misunderstood the task, overlooked another cue or brought an expectation from a previous page. A neutral follow-up question can help clarify their reasoning. Avoid telling the reader which feature you hope they will criticise. The value of the exercise lies in evidence about their interpretation, not in collecting agreement with a revision your group already prefers. Even a useful observation needs careful handling before it supports a specific design conclusion.

turns.speaker: Design host
turns.text: At the end of the workshop, compare your revised page with the original brief. Check each required output and note any remaining limitation. A page can be clearer than its first version while still omitting an essential detail. You should also identify one revision whose effect remains uncertain and explain how you would investigate it next. The closing review is not a request to declare the page perfect. It is a record of what changed, why it changed and what still needs attention before the material is used with its intended audience. That record makes a later update easier to justify than a page whose decisions survive only in one volunteer's memory.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: You completed both reader sessions last week. Today we're reviewing the draft before the next round.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: I still think the leaflet should include every fact in the background pack. Otherwise we might leave out something the client considers important.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: I disagree. We need to select information against the stated purpose, not assume every supplied fact is required.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: The proposal is to include all the background facts.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: Then I support it, perhaps in a compact section.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: I don't. A shorter relevant response would serve this brief better.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Keep the disagreement clear; it concerns selection from the supplied material, not whether accuracy matters.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Should the page state its intended audience explicitly?

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: At first I thought the audience would be obvious from the examples. The reader sessions showed that it wasn't. I support a short audience statement now.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: I agree. It would help visitors decide whether the activity is relevant before they work through the details.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What should that statement avoid?

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: It shouldn't promise that the activity suits every possible need.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Exactly. We can identify the group the page is written for and give a route for other enquiries.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then both of you support the statement, with a boundary that prevents a useful introduction from turning into an unsupported universal promise.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: One draft includes a number for expected attendance, but I can't find its source.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: I inserted an estimate because the space looked empty without a figure. That was a poor reason.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: I don't support inventing the number. We should state that attendance isn't yet confirmed or remove the claim.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Agreed. I'll delete the invented figure and mark the information gap.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Are you withdrawing the proposal to include a plausible estimate as though it were established?

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Yes, completely.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: We can discuss a clearly labelled scenario if the task genuinely needs one, but that would be a separate decision.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. The present draft should not disguise uncertainty as a precise-looking fact.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: The brief has an ambiguous criterion about length. Should you ask the client to clarify it before the next revision?

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: I support asking. We might waste the whole available period editing to a limit the client didn't intend.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: I'd state a reasonable assumption and produce a draft now, because the deadline is close and the client may not reply quickly.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Could you send the question while starting reversible work?

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Yes, but I still want clarification requested rather than silently settling the criterion ourselves.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: I understand, but for this next draft I would proceed with the explicit assumption.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then Tom supports the clarification request, while Saira retains a different approach to the time constraint.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Saira proposes a short opening summary.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: I support it because visitors could see the main action before reading the detail.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: I prefer going directly to headed steps. A summary might repeat information and use space we need for a condition that readers missed.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Would a single sentence change your view?

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: It might reduce the cost, but I still favour the headed steps without an extra summary.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: I continue to support one short sentence at the start.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Your reasons concern the distribution of attention and space. Neither proposal is automatically correct for every leaflet, so record what your next test would need to show to distinguish them.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What about keeping the uncertainty label beside the comparison figure?

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: We should keep it. Moving the qualification to a distant note would make the main figure look more certain than the evidence allows.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: I agree. I originally wanted a cleaner panel, but the label changes how the comparison should be read.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Can the wording be shortened?

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: Yes, provided the limitation remains clear.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: That's the version I support too.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then you both favour retaining a nearby qualification, not necessarily retaining every word of the current label.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: Exactly. We can improve readability without removing information that affects the meaning of the claim.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Which two checks are agreed for the revision procedure?

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: First, separate requirements from suggestions in the brief. In the earlier draft we treated a suggested example as compulsory and used too much space on it.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: Agreed. We should mark the wording that makes a requirement binding in this task.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Are you deciding to use every note in the background pack?

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: No, that remains a separate disagreement, not an agreed check.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: And adding an unrequested decorative chart isn't part of the procedure.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. The first check concerns the brief itself and should happen before you spend time polishing a response to a requirement that may not exist.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What is the second agreed check?

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: Link each section of the draft to a stated criterion. That would reveal a section that looks useful but doesn't answer any part of the task.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Yes, and it could also reveal a criterion with no corresponding section.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Will you predict a formal score for every section?

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: No. This is a local review against the brief, not a standardised assessment.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: The agreed checks are separating requirements from suggestions and connecting the draft to the criteria.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Keep that record short enough to use under the deadline. A checking process can itself become inefficient if it demands a long explanation of every minor formatting choice.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Which two limitations affect what you can claim from last week's reader sessions?

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: First, we didn't recruit people from the intended audience. The volunteers were classmates who already knew some of the terminology.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Agreed. Their responses can identify difficulties, but success with them doesn't prove that first-time visitors will understand the page.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Is printing in black and white necessarily a limitation here?

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: No, the material remained readable and the task didn't depend on colour.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: We also had access to the testing room, so its absence isn't an obstacle we experienced.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: State the audience mismatch specifically rather than describing the whole pilot as useless because it was small.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What is the second limitation?

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: The client changed part of the brief between the two sessions. We revised the page against a new requirement, not just against the first readers' comments.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: Yes. A difference between the sessions can't be attributed only to our wording changes.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What should the report preserve?

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: Both versions of the brief and a clear account of when the requirement changed.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: We shouldn't rewrite the earlier brief to make the development look tidier.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Exactly. The two limitations are the audience mismatch and the changed brief. The sessions occurred as scheduled, so a cancellation isn't another explanation for the results you observed.

parts.title: Turning a brief into a justified response

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: This lecture follows a fictional team responding to a short communication brief. The first stage defines the purpose. A purpose describes what the response should help its intended reader understand or do. A broad topic, such as a community event, is not yet a purpose. The team needs to specify whether the page explains an activity, enables a booking, compares options or supports another action. That decision shapes the information selected and the prominence given to it. Without a clear purpose, a page can become a collection of accurate facts that never helps the reader complete the task. Defining the purpose is therefore a practical design decision, not merely an introductory sentence in a planning document.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The second stage identifies the requirements in the brief. Requirements are the elements the response must satisfy, including any stated limits or conditions. The team distinguishes them from suggestions and examples, which may illustrate a possible approach without making it compulsory. If a requirement is genuinely ambiguous, the team records the question and seeks clarification when feasible. If it must proceed before receiving an answer, it makes the assumption visible. This is different from quietly choosing the easiest interpretation and later claiming it was the only possible reading. A clear requirements record helps the team explain why something appears in the response and why another attractive addition may reasonably be left out.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The third stage checks the evidence for the claims the response will make. Evidence may include supplied records, verified practical details or clearly identified observations from a local test. The team connects each important claim with the information supporting it. A statement can sound plausible while lacking the support needed for the intended use. Where a gap remains, the team can qualify the claim, obtain further information or leave it out. Inventing a precise figure is not a suitable way to make the page look complete. The purpose of this stage is to ensure that the response's apparent confidence does not exceed the information actually available to the people preparing it.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fourth stage produces a draft organised around the reader's task. A draft is a working version, so it can expose a problem without being treated as a final publication. The team chooses an order that makes the required action and its conditions easy to find. It also leaves room for the information that limits a claim, rather than treating every qualification as an inconvenient extra. During drafting, a team may discover that the brief asks for more than the available space can reasonably contain. That discovery should prompt a decision about priorities or clarification, not an attempt to solve every conflict by making the text smaller until the page becomes difficult to read.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fifth stage carries out a final validation against the brief. Validation is a check that the proposed response actually addresses the required task under the stated conditions. It includes looking for omitted outputs, unsupported claims and qualifications separated from the statements they limit. The check should not focus only on spelling or appearance, although those may also need attention. A polished response can still fail to answer the instruction. The team records any remaining issue rather than marking the whole task complete because the page has reached a convenient stopping point. This makes the decision to release or revise the draft easier to justify from evidence about what the response contains.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Relevance concerns the connection between information and the task. A detail may be accurate and interesting without helping the intended reader make the required decision. The team should ask why that detail deserves space in this response, rather than assume accuracy alone makes it necessary. The answer may depend on context: background information that is essential for a new visitor could be redundant for an experienced member. Relevance is therefore not a universal list of facts to include or exclude. It is a judgement linked to purpose, audience and the action being supported. Making that link explicit helps reviewers disagree productively instead of treating a preference for more or fewer words as a complete argument.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Proportionality concerns how much attention a point receives relative to its role in the task. A minor optional detail should not occupy so much space that a central requirement becomes difficult to find. At the same time, a short qualification can be crucial if it changes the meaning of a prominent claim. The team considers position, length and emphasis together. Reducing every section by the same percentage may preserve an existing imbalance rather than improve it. A proportionate response allocates attention according to the work the information needs to do. It doesn't necessarily make all sections equal, and it doesn't assume that the longest section is always the most important one.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Assumptions should remain visible when they affect the response. A team might assume that readers know a term, can access a link or will encounter the page before a certain date. Those assumptions may be reasonable for a defined audience, but they should not disappear from the reasoning merely because they make the design easier. The review asks which assumptions have been checked and which still need investigation. If a key assumption proves wrong, the appropriate revision may involve the structure of the task rather than a minor wording change. Recording assumptions helps the next reviewer understand why a design worked under one set of conditions and failed under another.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Limitations describe what the evidence or response cannot establish. A small reader test may reveal a confusing label without proving that a revised page will work for every visitor. The team should state that boundary clearly and connect it to the actual method used. A general apology for having limited time is less useful than explaining who was tested, what they were asked to do and which conditions differed from the intended use. Limitations do not require abandoning every practical decision. They help the team choose a next step that is proportionate to what it knows, such as another small test rather than an immediate broad claim that the design problem has been solved.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Finally, the team plans a follow-up to check whether the revision worked under the intended conditions. A follow-up is a later check, with a question and a defined way to gather evidence. It should not simply ask whether everyone liked the new appearance. The team might examine whether readers now find a required condition or can explain the action they need to take. The review records when the check will happen and which result would lead to another revision. This connects the present decision to future learning without pretending that the future result is already known. A completed draft can therefore remain part of an unfinished investigation whose next stage is clear and manageable.
